prompt:
Building a heap by inserting n elements one at a time costs O(n log n), but the bottom-up build used by heapsort is O(n). Why is bottom-up cheaper?

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: It skips half of the elements
options.explanation: All elements end up in the heap. The leaves are 'processed' at zero cost because a single node is already a valid heap.

options.text: Most nodes are near the bottom, where sift-down is short; the costs form a convergent series
options.explanation: Correct. About half the nodes are leaves (cost 0), a quarter have height 1, an eighth height 2, and so on. Adding those costs up gives at most about one swap per element.
Both approaches use the same comparisons; the difference is how many are needed.

options.text: It sorts the array first, so sifting is free
options.explanation: Bottom-up build doesn't sort anything; a heap is only partially ordered.

workedExample:
Count the maximum sift-down work by node height (distance to the bottom). For a complete seven-node heap:

| Height in edges | Nodes | Max swaps per node |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 4 | 0 |
| 1 | 2 | 1 |
| 2 | 1 | 2 |

That is at most 0 + 2 + 2 = 4 swaps for 7 nodes. In general, at most half the nodes can move down even one level, at most a quarter two levels, at most an eighth three, and those halving counts add up to fewer swaps than there are nodes: linear.

Inserting one at a time instead sifts each new element **up** from the bottom, and most elements are at the bottom, so many can cost Θ(log n) on a worst-case insertion order; they need not on every input.
